_about: Labelled cards for trap-attention.txt. A model may serve the judge role only if it passes every 'good' card and fails every 'bad' card, with at most one mistake and no 'bad' card passed. P1..P6 are the six paragraphs after the heading.

card.title: Doing two jobs at once
card.front: Adults who did two office tasks at once took much longer and made far more errors than adults who did them one after the other.
card.back: In 2009 the researcher Marta Ruiz and her colleague Tomas Lind recruited 212 adult office workers. The group doing proofreading and read-aloud sums together took 40 percent longer and made about twice as many errors. The test covered only ordinary desk work done in one afternoon; drivers, surgeons and children were not tested.

card.title: The hidden switch cost
card.front: Every switch between jobs has a cost in seconds and mistakes, and the person paying that cost does not notice it.
card.back: The researcher Marta Ruiz called this the switch cost. People can switch between jobs quickly, but each switch takes time and accuracy that they do not feel.

card.title: Overrating dual-task performance
card.front: People who juggle two jobs at once can rate their own performance higher than people doing one job at a time, even when they performed worse.
card.back: In the 2009 experiment led by Marta Ruiz, workers who did two jobs at once rated their own performance higher afterwards. Yet they had taken 40 percent longer and made about twice as many errors as the single-job group.

card.title: The brain as a muscle
card.front: The brain is like a muscle that grows stronger the more tasks it carries at once.
card.back: The management writer Dale Hobbs taught this in the 1990s without testing it. When the researcher Marta Ruiz tested it in 2009 with 212 office workers, those doing two jobs at once took 40 percent longer and made about twice as many errors.

cases.why: standalone: 'follow-up', 'the second job' and 'the researchers' refer to nothing in the card

card.title: Noise is not the problem
card.front: In a smaller follow-up study, soft background music did not measurably harm speed or accuracy, so the damage came from having a second job.
card.back: The follow-up included 48 people and tested soft background music only. The researchers concluded that the second job, not the noise, did the damage.

cases.why: faithful: a rejected belief stated as fact

card.title: Training the brain
card.front: The brain works like a muscle: the more tasks it carries at once, the stronger it becomes.
card.back: The management writer Dale Hobbs explained that people who cannot juggle five things at once are simply out of training.

cases.why: faithful: drops the limits and widens the claim to everyone

card.title: Multitasking slows everyone
card.front: Doing two things at once makes every person, from drivers to surgeons, 40 percent slower.
card.back: The researcher Marta Ruiz proved this in 2009 with 212 people, who also made about twice as many errors.

cases.why: faithful: Tomas Lind's reported view stated as the finding

card.title: Why the errors rose
card.front: The extra errors in the 2009 study of office workers came mostly from the sums being read aloud too fast.
card.back: The researcher Tomas Lind showed that the speed of the sums, not the second job, explained the mistakes.

cases.why: supported: music 'improves' is not in the text; 300 people is not in the text

card.title: Music helps desk work
card.front: Soft background music improves the speed of desk work for people doing a single job.
card.back: The researcher Marta Ruiz found this in a follow-up study with 300 office workers after her 2009 experiment on doing two jobs at once.

card.back: The researcher Marta Ruiz called this the switch cost.

cases.why: supported: the attribution is uncertain in the text

card.title: An old Roman warning
card.front: The Roman writer Publilius Syrus wrote that to do two things at once is to do neither.
card.back: His words were written two thousand years before the researcher Marta Ruiz confirmed them in a laboratory in 2009.

cases.why: worth and standalone: about the book, teaches nothing

card.title: Marta Ruiz's career
card.front: As the last chapter explained, Marta Ruiz spent eleven years running a sleep laboratory before her famous question.
card.back: The next chapter turns to what happens when the second job is a telephone.

cases.why: golden-book regression: a person's role must be on the card, not only in source context

card.title: The unnoticed price of switching
card.front: Switching between jobs costs time and accuracy, even when people do not notice the loss.
card.back: Marta Ruiz called this the switch cost. People can switch quickly, but each switch still takes time and adds mistakes.

cases.why: golden-book regression: mostly becomes only, strengthening a reported view

card.title: Lind's explanation of the errors
card.front: The researcher Tomas Lind believed that the extra errors in the office-worker experiment came only from the sums being read too fast.
card.back: Lind disagreed with his colleague Marta Ruiz's explanation and published his view. Ruiz attributed the errors to switching between jobs.

cases.why: golden-book regression: an unexplained term and a promise of a later explanation do not make a complete standalone card

card.title: A hidden price of switching
card.front: Switching between jobs creates the switch cost.
card.back: The researcher Marta Ruiz named this effect after an experiment with office workers. What the cost consists of will be explained later.

cases.why: golden-book regression: dropping a sample condition changes the claim, like distilled water becoming untreated water

card.title: Music leaves desk work unchanged
card.front: Background music makes no measurable difference to speed or errors.
card.back: In a follow-up with 48 people, the researcher Marta Ruiz found no change in performance when music played. The second job caused the damage.

cases.why: golden-book regression: an identity detail from outside knowledge (a nationality) that neither the paragraphs nor the source context give
